The view from Earth, 4.5 billion years to today

What could be seen from the ground at nineteen moments in Earth's history: the color of the sky, straight up and at the horizon, at the equator and the poles, at noon and at dusk, reconstructed with a spectral radiative-transfer model; and the Sun, Moon, planets, stars and everything else above it, from the molten newborn Moon to a sky full of satellites.

Ten things the view did

  1. Under the 30-bar CO₂ of the early Hadean the sky was a shadowless peach-white glow with no visible Sun, and the molten newborn Moon, 4° across and 8 Earth radii away, glowed orange through it, rising and setting several times in a 6-hour day.
  2. During the hazy Neoarchean the whole dome was cream to apricot, with almost no difference between zenith and horizon.
  3. Before the Great Oxidation every twilight ended in a cream zenith; the first ozone turned it pale blue, and the deep blue dusk needs a near-modern column.
  4. Snowball Earth had the bluest sky in Earth's history; the K–Pg impact winter had no sunsets at all.
  5. The eclipsed Moon is copper today, orange-rimmed before there was ozone, dark-cored when the Moon was close, and gone under the K–Pg soot, the thick Archean haze or a Tambora veil.
  6. Before the Great Oxidation the nights were darker and violet: no oxygen airglow, nitrogen aurorae reaching the mid-latitudes, and meteors with no glowing trains.
  7. The young Sun was smaller, redder and dimmer, and so heavily spotted that a spot could be seen on it every day.
  8. The Moon's face was not always today's: at 3.8 Ga the maria were still flooding, and at 4.0 Ga the near side was bright highland from limb to limb.
  9. Saturn had no rings before about 160 million years ago, and θ Columbae, now a faint fifth-magnitude star, shone as bright as Venus 4.7 million years ago.
  10. In 2100 thousands of orbital datacenters may outshine nearly every star at dusk, in a bright band along the terminator.

1. Introduction

What did the sky look like from the ground in the Archean, under the young Sun, with the Moon nearer? We reconstruct the whole view from Earth's surface at nineteen moments in its history, from a proto-Earth 17 million years after the first solids to the year 2100: the color of the sky by day and at dusk, computed with a spectral radiative-transfer model of each epoch's air, and on that sky everything else that could be seen from the ground: the Sun and its spots, the Moon's size, face and eclipses, the planets and their moons, the stars and the Galaxy as they then lay, meteors, comets, aurorae, airglow, halos and clouds, and in the latest epochs the light people added. It began as a study of the sky's color, which remains its quantitative core, and grew with the interactive site built on the model, which draws each of these and is the source of every number quoted here outside the color tables.

The nineteen epochs (Table 1) were chosen for what changed: the air (a 30-bar CO₂ Hadean, an Archean with no oxygen and organic haze, the first ozone after the Great Oxidation, a frozen Snowball, the oxygen-rich Carboniferous, the impact winter after Chicxulub, a volcanic year, the ozone hole and today's cities), the sky above it (a Moon forming and receding, a young and active Sun, a Solar System before the giant planets' instability, nearby supernovae, stars that outshone Sirius, a bombardment and a possible ring), and the view people have made (city light and a sky full of satellites). Each is a reconstruction, with the uncertainties the sections state: some quantities are measured, some modeled, some estimated to show a trend, and some, like where the planets stood on a given day four billion years ago, unknowable and drawn at random.

This is a living document. Much of what it draws rests on questions that are still argued: when the giant planets went unstable and whether a fifth giant was lost; how far away the Moon was in its first hundred million years; how thick the Archean haze was and how much ozone the first oxygen made; how old Saturn's rings are; whether the Earth had a ring in the Ordovician; how bright the young Sun's corona and wind were. Where the literature disagrees, we say which reading we take and why, and as the consensus moves the site and this report will move with it: epochs will be redrawn, numbers revised and new findings added. Each version carries its date, and the code and data that produce it are public, so any figure here can be traced to the model and the sources behind it.

The site computes what it shows as realistically as it can while still loading in seconds and running smoothly in a browser, and where the two conflict it compromises. Some compromises stand in for physics too costly to run. Jupiter's and Saturn's clouds are a tracer stirred by a flow made of noise, shaped by the measured winds and rolled into eddies and billows, a proxy for the planets' true three-dimensional hydrodynamics rather than a simulation of it; the animation repeats over a 2000-day cycle. The sky's multiple scattering is a two-stream approximation rather than a full Monte Carlo transfer, computed ahead of time on a grid of Sun heights and interpolated between them. The clouds are scenery, procedural volumes lit by the model's sky rather than the output of a climate model, and the Milky Way is a model of its structure rather than a photograph. The photosphere's granulation and the Moon's craters' shadows are drawn from procedural cells and a limited march toward the Sun, and the close-up detail of Jupiter, Saturn, the Sun and the spacecraft maps is built only when the view zooms in on them. Other compromises are made for the eye: the Sun and Moon are drawn at four times their size, the sunset's colors are spread further apart than they are, and the Sun's limb darkening is softened. Each section says where its subject is measured, modeled or approximated.

In Section 2 we describe how the view is reconstructed. Section 3 gives the sky's colors by day and at dusk, and Section 4 through Section 9 take in turn the Sun, the Moon, the planets, the stars and the Galaxy, the night and what crosses it, and the sky people made. Section 10 goes through the epochs one by one, and Section 11 says what the reconstruction leaves out and which of its numbers are estimates.

1.1 Has this been done before?

Not as such. A search of the Valency corpus (arXiv, PubMed, EarthArXiv and others) finds the two halves of the sky-color problem solved separately but never joined. On one side, atmospheric-optics work computes modern sky color rigorously: Lynch & Mazuk (2005) derive CIE chromaticities of the sky, Sun and distant objects from MODTRAN spectra; Peyvandi et al. (2016) simulate 5.6 million daylight spectra with SBDART to map how aerosol and ozone shift sky color; Lee & Mollner (2017) show with Monte Carlo simulation that vivid solar-horizon twilight colors need aerosol while the purest antisolar colors occur in a purely molecular atmosphere. On the other side, paleoatmosphere work constrains composition: Catling & Zahnle (2020) for the Archean (O₂ below 10⁻⁶ of present, CO₂ 10–2,500× modern, CH₄ 10²–10⁴× modern), and Arney et al. (2016), Mak et al. (2023) and Goldblatt et al. (2024) for the organic-haze episodes. Arney's “Pale Orange Dot” computes what a hazy Archean Earth looks like from space, as an exoplanet spectrum, and Sanromà & Pallé (2012) its light curves through history; that is as close as the literature comes. Nobody has computed the view from the ground, or the horizon-versus-zenith, latitude, and sunset structure.

The same holds for the rest of the view. Its pieces are separate results: the Moon's recession and the day's lengthening (Farhat et al. 2022), the young Sun's brightness and activity, the stars' past motions, the giant planets' early instability. Earth's transmission spectrum has been computed through geological time as a transiting exoplanet would show it (Kaltenegger, Lin & Madden 2020), and today's lunar eclipse has been modeled with refraction (García Muñoz et al. 2012), but no reconstruction of how the eclipsed Moon itself looked in past epochs turns up, nor of how these pieces together looked from the ground on a given evening. We assemble them here.

2. How the view is reconstructed

2.1 The sky's colors

For each epoch the atmosphere is built from components with their own vertical profile and spectral optical depth: Rayleigh-scattering gas (N₂, O₂, CO₂, CH₄, H₂O in their epoch-appropriate partial pressures), ozone (the Chappuis cross section of Serdyuchenko et al. 2014 at 223 K, on a layer whose peak falls from 26 km at the equator to 18 km at the pole), tropospheric aerosol, a stratospheric sulfate layer, a tholin-like fractal organic haze (strongly blue-absorbing, forward-scattering), and impact soot (Table 2). Sky radiance is integrated numerically along each line of sight through a spherical-shell atmosphere, so grazing sunlight at twilight is handled properly, with multiple scattering and surface reflection added from a delta-Eddington two-stream solution. Spectra from 380–780 nm are converted to CIE XYZ with the analytic color-matching functions of Wyman, Sloan & Shirley (2013) and shown as sRGB. The model reproduces measured modern values (clear zenith 10,000–20,000 K, horizon 6,000–8,500 K, setting Sun ~1,700 K, pink antisolar Belt of Venus) before being pointed backward.

We treat the young Sun as a blackbody whose effective temperature and luminosity follow the solar track of Baraffe et al. (2015): 5,530 K and 68% of today's output at 4.5 Ga, rising through 5,620 K (75%) at 3.8 Ga, 5,660 K (80%) at 2.7 Ga and 5,700 K (85%) at 2.2 Ga to 5,772 K today, and 4,614 K (47%) for the 17-million-year-old Sun of 4.55 Ga. The color effect is small: a 5,560 K Sun is only about 200 K cooler in color temperature than the modern one, a difference that is barely perceptible side by side and is swamped by atmospheric effects ten to a hundred times larger. The brightness effect is not small, and is why the early-epoch skies are rendered dimmer. We ignore Fraunhofer lines and the young Sun's ultraviolet excess, which matter for haze photochemistry but not for visible color. The model is provided as the Python source skymodel.py; run_epochs.py produces the sky colors and limb_grid.py the limb and disk colors.

2.2 The rest of the view

The sky's colors come from the radiative-transfer model described above; the rest of the view is drawn on them by the interactive site, in two views: a dome, the whole sky as a fisheye, and a first-person view in WebGL, with a walkable ground and clouds. Both draw on one photometric scale, calibrated in absolute units: the clear zenith with the Sun 45° up is 2.7 kcd/m², which puts the full-Moon sky at the measured 18 mag/arcsec². Stars, planets, meteors and satellites are placed by their magnitudes on that scale and dimmed by the epoch's air, 0.15 magnitude per airmass from the gas plus 1.086 times its aerosol or haze optical depth; each shows only when it is brighter than the naked-eye limit for the sky around it. The Moon, moonlight, supernovae, fireballs and city glow light the sky through the same model. The clock runs over one solar day of the epoch, and the Sun follows the seasons for the date with today's 23.4° tilt in every epoch, since the Moon has held the obliquity between about 22° and 24.5°. The Sun and Moon are drawn at four times their angular size so that their disks show on a screen, and zooming in acts as a telescope, down to a field of 14 arcseconds.

Where each body was is carried back as far as it can be known. The Moon's distance follows the tidal record, the Sun's brightness and size its evolutionary track, the stars their measured motions back to the Pleistocene and orbits in a model Galaxy to 66 Ma; beyond that the star field and the planets' positions are drawn at random, with the right statistics, since no calculation can recover them. The colors are shown as a daylight-balanced camera would record them, without chromatic adaptation, and the night as a dark-adapted eye sees it. The scenery and the clouds are drawn, not modeled; the sky is the model.

2.3 The ground

The ground is scenery, like the clouds: a walkable landscape chosen for each era rather than computed, lit by the model's sky and Sun. The proto-Earth has magma pools; the 4.5 Ga Earth a hot ocean, about 200 °C under 30 bar of CO₂ (Zahnle et al. 2010), steaming round volcanic islands; the Archean, water and volcanic shields; Snowball Earth, ice plateaus with blue banded cliffs and frozen ponds; the Ordovician, shallow seas with no land plants beyond mosses and crusts; the Carboniferous, forest and swamps; the impact winter, dead woods; the Pleistocene, 1815 and today, woods and snow-capped peaks; and the modern epochs, a town with lit windows. Water reflects the sky and glitters in the Sun and Moon; lava glows; distant scenery fades into the sky's color. None of this is part of the model: the sky above it is.

3.1 Horizon versus zenith

In a clean molecular atmosphere the zenith is blue and the horizon white because the horizon path is long enough that blue is scattered back out before reaching the eye and multiple scattering fills in the other colors. The size of that gradient is the clearest single diagnostic of atmospheric state. It is largest in the cleanest atmospheres (Snowball Earth, today's clean air: 8,000–13,000 K of color-temperature difference), shrinks as Rayleigh depth rises (late Hadean), collapses to nothing when a broadband absorber or thick scatterer sits overhead (hazy Archean, impact winter, 30-bar Hadean), and actually reverses under a stratospheric sulfate veil or heavy pollution, where the zenith becomes whiter than the horizon.

3.2 Equator, mid-latitudes, poles

Latitude enters through solar elevation and surface albedo. A high Sun lights the sky from above through a short path, giving a brighter but paler zenith (equatorial noon ~9,000 K); a low Sun sends light through more air, so the polar summer zenith is a deeper, darker blue (~19,000 K today, 20,000 K over Snowball ice) while the polar horizon is warmer and yellower. The same geometry makes the poles the place where any overhead absorber is most visible: the hazy Archean sky is cream at the equator but distinctly orange-yellow at the poles, and the impact-winter Sun that is still a pale disk at the equator is gone at 75° latitude. Snow and ice brighten and blue-shift the whole dome by reflecting light back into the atmosphere, which is why polar and Snowball horizons stay blue where a mid-latitude land horizon goes white.

3.3 Particulates

Three kinds of particle appear in the record, and each leaves a different sky. Non-absorbing sulfate high in the stratosphere (volcanic years) whitens the day sky and produces long, luminous pink and lavender twilights, because the layer is still sunlit after the ground is dark. Absorbing organic haze (Neoarchean) or soot (impact winter) removes blue outright, turning the dome tan or amber with almost no directional structure, and dims the surface by factors of 3–20. Boundary-layer pollution or dust brightens and grays the zenith, and buries the setting Sun in murk before it reaches the horizon. Tropospheric aerosol is also what makes sunset color vivid: the model confirms Lee & Mollner's result that a purely molecular sky yields a pale, yellow-orange horizon while any turbidity deepens it to red.

3.4 Sunsets and sunrises through time

The biggest surprise is ozone. Today the sky above a setting Sun grades from orange through pale yellow to a zenith that stays blue well into twilight: about 12,500 K with the Sun 4° down. That persistent blue is the Chappuis band, ozone absorbing yellow and orange along the grazing path. The same modern sky with the ozone removed drops that zenith to cream, about 6,000 K. Before the Great Oxidation Event there was no ozone, so every sunset for the first two billion years ended with the zenith fading through cream and beige to orange. At ~2.2 Ga a 66 DU column, the Cooke et al. (2022) global mean for 1% of present oxygen, turns that cream zenith a pale blue-gray near 7,100 K. The deep twilight blue arrives later, once the column is near modern: the snowball sky, at their 10% oxygen column of 169 DU, holds a dusk zenith near 10,800 K. The same thinning is visible in the ozone-hole years. A polar-spring column of 130 DU leaves the dusk zenith pale blue, near 7,800 K, against 12,500 K today. Beyond the ozone story: Hadean sunsets were not events at the horizon but a slow dimming of the whole glowing dome; hazy Archean sunsets were the longest and most saturated in Earth's history, vermilion at the horizon and amber overhead; Snowball sunsets were brief and golden; the sunsets of the impact winter did not exist as color at all; and the reddest, most theatrical skies of the Phanerozoic belong to volcanic years like 1815 and 1883.

3.5 The atmosphere from space

To show latitude and altitude at once, these renderings look at Earth from space with the Sun behind the viewer at the equinox, so the solar zenith angle at every point equals its latitude (equator at the center line, poles at top and bottom). The shell around the disk is the atmosphere's limb: the color of light scattered toward the viewer along a tangent ray at each altitude, computed with the same model. The atmosphere is drawn 30 times too thick, so 100 km spans half an Earth radius; a real limb is a hairline. The disk shows the planet's reflected color over a dark ocean (over ice for Snowball Earth), with limb brightness compressed so faint upper layers remain visible.

Equinox geometry with the Sun behind the viewer; the shell is the limb color along tangent rays, drawn 30 times too thick (100 km spans half an Earth radius); the disk is the planet's reflected color over ocean (ice for Snowball Earth). Limb brightness is compressed so faint upper layers remain visible.

3.6 Clouds

Clouds are not part of the radiative-transfer model; the first-person view draws them as scenery, ray-marched through a volume and lit by the model's sky, the Sun and the Moon, and by a supernova, a fireball or city light when there is one. Their regimes are illustrative choices for each era rather than results: a near-overcast stratiform deck under the steamy Hadean CO₂ (88% cover at 4.5 Ga), scattered cumulus in the Archean thinning as the haze thickens (from 48% at 3.8 Ga to 16% under the thickest haze), sparse thin cloud over the frozen Snowball (22%), towering convection in the warm Carboniferous (82%), almost none in the impact winter (8%), and more cirrus in the volcanic year. The weather changes over days and the clouds through each day: cumulus eras build to an afternoon peak and stratiform ones burn off by midday. After sunset the clouds stay lit from below until the Earth's shadow climbs past them.

3.7 Crepuscular rays

Where the Sun shines from behind a cloud, beams fan out across the sky and the sky between them darkens: crepuscular rays, the cloud's shadow in the sunlit air. Only the part of each direction's light that is sunlight scattered once in the lower air can be shadowed, so the page computes that share from each epoch's own air, its gas, aerosol, dust, haze, sulfate and soot layers with their heights, for every Sun height and direction (shafts.py); along each line of sight the stretches whose path to the Sun passes through cloud lose their share. The rays are strongest where the scattering sits low, and weakest in the 30-bar Hadean, whose light is multiply scattered and comes from everywhere at once. The Moon makes the same rays through gaps in cloud, and so does a bright fireball.

3.8 Ice halos

In clear, very cold air the sky fills with diamond dust, tiny hexagonal plates and columns of ice drifting near the ground. Snowball Earth's air would have been full of them at every latitude. Today they are common on the Antarctic plateau and in Arctic winter, so they are drawn at 75° in the modern epochs and in the other cold epochs (2.2 Ga at the end of the Huronian glaciations, the Late Ordovician and Late Paleozoic ice ages, and the Pleistocene), and faintly at 45° at 342 ka, a glacial maximum.

The halos are traced from the crystals' geometry with the refractive index of ice at 450, 550 and 650 nm (Warren & Brandt 2008), so each arc carries its own dispersion, red toward the Sun: the 22° and 46° halos, the upper and lower tangent arcs, the sun dogs (which move out with the Sun's height and vanish above 61°), the circumzenithal arc (only while the Sun is below 32°), the parhelic circle with its 120° parhelia, a sun pillar for a low Sun, and the diffraction aureole. The Moon makes the same, faintly. Their brightness, set against the clean noon sky, is an estimate of a good display; the air in front of them is each epoch's.

4. The Sun

4.1 The young Sun

The Sun has brightened by about 30% since the Earth formed, as hydrogen burning has raised the density and temperature of its core. We follow the 1 M☉ track of Baraffe et al. (2015): 68% of today's light and 5,530 K at 4.5 Ga, 80% and 5,660 K at 2.7 Ga, 94% at 700 Ma, today's 5,772 K by the Cenozoic. Its radius follows from the luminosity and temperature: 0.90 of today's at 4.5 Ga, 0.93 at 2.7 Ga, 0.98 at 700 Ma, so the young Sun's disk was smaller as well as dimmer, and the closer Moon covered it easily. The 4.55 Ga Sun is different. Seventeen million years old, it is still contracting onto the main sequence: cooler, 4,614 K, at 47% of today's light but 7% larger than today's, an orange-white disk. The color change is small, two or three hundred kelvin for most of the record, and swamped by the air's; the brightness change is not, and it is why the early skies are drawn dimmer. The Earth–Sun distance varies through the year with today's eccentricity, so the Sun is 3.4% brighter at perihelion in January.

4.2 Sunspots

The Sun's disk carries its spots and faculae, drawn from a map of the whole photosphere made for each epoch and day and turned with the Sun's rotation. How spotted the Sun was follows its age. Young solar analogs are spotted over 1 to 10% of their surface, the coverage falling roughly as the inverse square root of age (Morris 2020) and much faster once the rotation period passes about 15 days (Nichols-Fleming & Blackman 2020). Stars more active than Rossby number one, the Sun before about 2.5 Gyr, dim when they are active: dark spots dominate their variability. Older, quieter stars like today's Sun brighten with activity, dominated by bright faculae (Shapiro et al. 2014; Reinhold et al. 2019), because spot area grows faster with activity than facular area does (Nemec et al. 2022). The Sun's rotation follows the slow-rotator sequence it most likely took (Gallet & Bouvier 2013): 3.1 days at 4.5 Ga, 16 at 2.7 Ga, 23 at 700 Ma.

Fast rotators carry spots at high latitudes and large cool polar caps, as Doppler images of young solar analogs show (Barnes et al. 2005), so the Hadean and early Archean Suns have their spots between 10° and 75° and caps round the poles. A regular cycle sets in at a few hundred million years (Katsova 2020); from 2.7 Ga the spots emerge in a butterfly pattern, from mid-latitudes toward the equator over each cycle (Hathaway 2011), on cycles lengthening from 8 to 11 years. On Gregorian dates the modern epochs follow the real cycles, each cycle's sunspot number from the SILSO record with the shape of Hathaway, Wilson & Reichmann (1994): the 1815 volcanic year falls in the Dalton Minimum and dates in the Maunder Minimum are all but spotless. Beyond the record a sixth of the time is a grand minimum, as over the Holocene (Usoskin, Solanki & Kovaltsov 2007).

Each active region is a bipolar group: a large, round leading spot ahead in the rotation and nearer the equator (Joy's law), a following polarity broken into smaller spots, often with partial penumbrae, and pores between. Peak areas are lognormal (Baumann & Solanki 2005); a group grows in days and decays linearly, faster the smaller it is, and drifts with the latitude's rotation (Snodgrass 1983). The spots have the structure seen in white light (Solanki 2003; Borrero & Ichimoto 2011): an umbra of 3,700 to 4,600 K, darker the larger it is, sprinkled with umbral dots and crossed in the larger spots by granular light bridges; a penumbra of radial filaments 150 to 650 K below the photosphere, with bright grains at their inner ends and a ragged, comb-like outer edge; and round the region, faculae that show only toward the limb, cleared from a moat round each mature spot, over the faint network of the supergranulation. Intensities are Planck ratios at the color channels' wavelengths, so spots are redder as well as darker. The disk is drawn as a white-light photograph is shown, with umbrae near-black and penumbrae mid-gray. Zoomed further, past the map's resolution of about 1,000 km, the photosphere's own fine structure takes over (The Sun close up).

A spot about an arcminute across, some 500 millionths of the hemisphere, is the smallest the eye can see unaided through a haze or a filter (Vaquero 2007). Today one is on the disk about one day in 25, mostly near solar maximum; in the Proterozoic every other day; in the Archean and Hadean always, about 30 at once at 4.5 Ga. Spots then take about 3% off the Sun's light, and they gather toward the poles, darkening the top and bottom of the disk. The young Sun's shape does not change visibly: rotating in 3 days flattens it by only 0.05%, and even a 1-day rotation by 0.5%, 5 arcseconds on a 32-arcminute disk.

4.3 The Sun close up

Zoomed in, down to a field of view of 14 arcseconds, the photosphere is drawn as high-resolution solar telescopes show it: granulation, convection cells about 1,300 km across, bright where hot gas rises and dark in the narrow lanes where it sinks, living about eight minutes, a fifth of the larger ones splitting from a dark knot late in life (exploding granules); magnetic bright points a couple of hundred kilometers across in the lanes inside faculae; penumbral filaments a few thousand kilometers long; umbral dots about 1,000 K hotter than the umbra around them; and toward the limb the supergranular network, cells some 30,000 km across outlined by brightenings. Spot and plage edges are ragged down to the pixel. This fine structure is the same in every epoch; only the spots and faculae change with the Sun's age (Figure 5).

In the first-person view a Sun near full daylight is not drawn as a disk at all but as the eye sees it: a blinding white blank tinted the epoch's color, in a bloom that whitens the sky around it. Zooming in, as through a filter, dims it to the real disk, and the glare eases off as the Sun sets or is eclipsed, until the corona and Baily's beads take over.

4.4 The setting Sun

Near the horizon the Sun is drawn as twenty images, one per 20 nm band from 385 to 765 nm, each lifted by its own refraction (the dispersion of air, Edlén 1966) and dimmed by its own optical depth along the grazing path through the epoch's model atmosphere. At the horizon the green and orange images of today's Sun are only about 6 arcseconds apart, so the colors separate only in the last sliver: the green flash is whichever band survives the extinction last, and the cleaner the air the shorter that wavelength. Along the horizontal path, the model's air still passes a twentieth of its peak sunlight at 550 nm in the clean, dry Snowball epoch, the best flashes in the record, and at 630 nm in today's clean air; under the Neoarchean haze, the impact-winter soot, a volcanic veil or a polluted city nothing shorter than 650 to 730 nm gets through, and there is no flash at all.

How far the air lifts the Sun follows its refractivity, the sum over its gases' partial pressures. Today's horizon refraction of about 34 arcminutes is 1.8 times larger at 4.0 Ga (half a bar of CO₂ on a bar of N₂), 1.11 times in the oxygen-rich Carboniferous and 0.83 times in Snowball Earth's thinner air, so the Sun sets later or earlier by a minute or two. The 30-bar Hadean air is 47 times as refractive as today's: a horizontal ray bends faster than the ground curves and is trapped (ducting), but its Sun is lost in Rayleigh scattering long before it reaches the horizon, so we hold the drawn bending to three times today's.

Each evening also has its own layering of the low air, set by the date so that a given evening always sets the same way. Thin temperature inversions step the disk's edge, show a strip of it twice (once inverted) where the rays cross, and draw a dark line across it where trapped rays run through the densest air; over warm water the Sun meets its own inverted image in an inferior mirage, the “omega” sunset. The cold surface of Snowball Earth makes inversions common and inferior mirages rare, and the warm oceans of the Hadean and Archean the reverse. These mirage statistics are illustrative. The disk is also darker and redder toward its edge (limb darkening, Hestroffer & Magnan 1998): the air only multiplies the Sun's light, so the darkening is the same under every sky.

Two of these effects are drawn larger than life. The disk itself is drawn at four times its angular size, as the Moon is, so that it shows at all on a screen, and the bands' separation by refraction is enlarged with it, four times high in the sky and up to 24 times at the horizon, where a real flash is a sliver of a few arcseconds. And the limb darkening is drawn at a fifth of its true strength: on a disk drawn near white, the real contrast reads as a dark rim. The spectrum readout keeps the full law.

4.5 Solar eclipses

When the Moon covers part of the Sun, all the sunlit sky dims by the fraction of the disk still showing. In totality the sky is lit from beyond the Moon's shadow, tens to a hundred kilometers away, where the Sun is still partly up: the epoch's own twilight sky with a sunset glow all round the horizon, a thousandth of the day sky, as measured (Sharp, Lloyd & Silverman 1966). The Hadean and hazy Archean totality skies are therefore that era's dusk, peach or amber rather than the deep blue of a modern eclipse.

The corona follows the Sun's age. A younger Sun spun faster and was far more active: its X-ray output goes as age to the −1.5 (Güdel, Guinan & Skinner 1997), about 530 times today's at 4.5 Ga, and its coronal temperature with it, 7.7 MK against 1.5 MK. Today's corona (Baumbach 1937: electron-scattered K light near the limb, dust-scattered F light beyond about 2.3 solar radii) is scaled accordingly: a denser, more extended K corona, an F corona that follows the era's zodiacal dust, stronger coronal lines (the green Fe XIV and red Fe X, joined by yellow Ca XV in the hot young corona) and a brighter pink chromosphere. These scalings are estimates. The young Sun was also smaller (0.90 of today's radius at 4.5 Ga) while the Moon was closer, so early eclipses hide the inner corona: at 3.8 Ga the Moon looks 1.5 times the Sun's width, and from 2.2 Ga back every central eclipse is total. Through the 30-bar Hadean air, at 7.6 magnitudes of extinction per airmass, the corona does not show at all. The proto-Earth of 4.55 Ga has no Moon, and so no eclipses; its Sun, 17 million years old, has the saturated corona of a star that young, at about 9 MK.

The eclipse itself is drawn from the Moon's real profile: at second and third contact the last sunlight breaks into Baily's beads where the lunar limb's valleys, from the Laser Altimeter's heights, let the photosphere through, and a diamond ring. Like the disks, the eclipses are enlarged: the Sun and Moon are drawn at four times their size, and eclipses are found and timed with the enlarged disks, so the page's partial phases last longer, and its eclipses happen at more places, than real ones. For each new Moon the page stands where parallax brings the Moon closest to the Sun, the best seat for that eclipse.

5. The Moon

5.1 The Moon's orbit through time

The Moon raises tides on the Earth, and the tidal bulge, carried ahead of it by the Earth's spin, pulls it forward: the Moon has been receding ever since it formed, today by 3.8 cm a year, while the Earth's day lengthens. Run back, the Moon was closer and bigger, its month shorter, and the day shorter too. We take the distance from Farhat et al. (2022), whose tidal model fits both the present recession and the geological record of tidal rhythmites, back to 3.2 Ga, where Eulenfeld & Heubeck (2023) find 70% of today's distance in the Moodies Group rhythmites; older ages extend the long-term drift. At 4.5 Ga, some ten million years after the giant impact, the Moon is still at about 8 Earth radii: Korenaga (2023) finds that a Moon whose magma ocean was still solidifying raised little tide in itself and had receded only to 7 to 9 Earth radii by the time the ocean froze. (Table 5 gives the numbers by epoch.)

The day follows from the distance by holding the Earth–Moon angular momentum fixed: a closer Moon means a faster-spinning Earth. This reproduces the day lengths Farhat et al. (2022) give for their distances to within a tenth of an hour, 21.9 hours at 700 Ma and 15.6 hours at 2.7 Ga, and at 4.5 Ga it gives 5.9 hours. The year is the same length in seconds in every epoch, since the Earth's orbit is set by the Sun's mass, which has barely changed; so a year held 400 days in Snowball Earth, 562 at 2.7 Ga and 1,486 at 4.5 Ga. The month, by Kepler's third law, was 22.6 of today's days at 2.2 Ga and 15.3 at 4.0 Ga, still 28 to 31 of each epoch's own shorter days; at 2.7 Ga a year held about eighteen months, as tidal rhythmites suggest. At 4.5 Ga the Moon went round in 32 hours, five and a half of that epoch's days. The proto-Earth of 4.55 Ga has no Moon; how fast it turned before the impact cannot be known, and its 12-hour day is a guess.

The orbit's tilt to the ecliptic also changed. We carry today's 5.15° back along these distances with the semi-analytic tidal model of Ćuk et al. (2016): the Earth's tides tilt the orbit less as the Moon recedes, and tides raised in the Moon itself damp the tilt, most strongly near 33 Earth radii, where the Moon's own obliquity swings large. The orbit comes out a little steeper in the past, 5.5° at 2.7 Ga and 5.8° at 4.0 Ga; Ćuk et al. argue these are lower bounds, and the 17° to 30° and more that such models give for the young Moon belong before 33 Earth radii, older than any epoch here but 4.5 Ga. Inside about 17 Earth radii the orbit precesses about the Earth's equator rather than the ecliptic (Tremaine, Touma & Namouni 2009), so the 4.5 Ga Moon is drawn in the plane of the equator. The orbit was more eccentric too, growing from today's 0.055 to about 0.1 at 4.0 Ga (Daher et al. 2021), after it had been through the evection resonance, which can raise it to 0.5 for a hundred thousand years (Ćuk & Stewart 2012), and been damped nearly round again by 4.5 Ga. With the eccentricity the Moon rocks east and west each month by about twice the eccentricity in radians, ±6.3° today and ±12° at 4.0 Ga, and north and south by its obliquity, 6.7° today and 21° to 23° at 3.8 and 4.0 Ga, as it nears the Cassini-state transition; the page draws the globe on these axes, so the Moon visibly librates.

The consequences show in the sky. At 3.8 Ga the Moon is one and a half times today's width and more than twice as bright when full. At 4.5 Ga it is 4° across, seven and a half times today's width and 56 times its area, and so close that it is placed as seen from the ground: it shifts 7° against the stars between the horizon and the zenith. It crosses the sky in hours, rising and setting several times a day. In the plane of the equator, it eclipses the Sun at every new Moon for weeks around each equinox, somewhere on the Earth, and passes through the Earth's shadow, 14° across at its distance, at every full Moon.

5.2 The Moon's face

The Moon's face is the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter's: the Wide Angle Camera's color mosaic, toned to match a full-Moon photograph, and the Laser Altimeter's heights (NASA's CGI Moon Kit). The heights light the slopes, cast shadows toward the terminator, and shape the limb, so a zoomed crescent shows a ragged terminator and crater shadows, and the edge of the Moon in an eclipse breaks the last sunlight into Baily's beads. Five globes cover the Moon's history (Figure 8). Tycho, 108 million years old (Arvidson et al. 1976), is taken away with its rays for the epochs older than 108 Ma. Before about 3.9 Ga the maria had not been flooded: basalts filled the great basins from about 3.9 Ga and most of them by 3.3 Ga (Hiesinger et al. 2011), so each mare darkens over 150 million years from an onset just before its oldest dated basalt. At 3.8 Ga Tranquillitatis is two-thirds dark, Serenitatis and Nectaris a third, and Imbrium and Procellarum are still bright: the familiar face is not there yet. At 4.0 Ga the near side is bright highland from limb to limb. At 3.8 Ga the eruptions themselves show: one to three fissure eruptions a lunation glow on the night side, a few to a hundred square kilometers of lava at about 1,400 K, as bright per area as the sunlit Moon and far redder, magnitude +3 to −1 as seen from the Earth.

The Moon of 4.5 Ga is not yet solid. Its magma ocean is open at the top, a few million years after the impact: rafts of dark quench crust and the first pale anorthosite, floating a few hundred meters to a kilometre and a half above the melt, broken by cracks and lava lakes at 1,400 to 1,600 K in four generations of floes, each a network of cracks within the last. The lava shines about as brightly per area as the sunlit Moon, so the disk glows orange by day and night alike, also inside the Earth's shadow, and the air around it carries a red aureole. The map and its relief are made up; that the young Moon looked like this is an inference from its magma ocean, not an observation.

The night side is drawn at a flat 6% of the lit side's brightness rather than with a modeled earthshine, which the spectrum readout gives instead: about 2 × 10⁻⁴ of the day side when the Earth is full from the Moon, and bluer.

5.3 Moonlight

Moonlight is the same sky model with the Moon in place of the Sun, scaled by the lunar phase (the Allen phase law with the opposition surge, as in Krisciunas & Schaefer 1991) and by the inverse square of the Moon's distance. It stays nearly the same in color from epoch to epoch but not in brightness: the full Moon lit the sky 2.2 times as brightly at 3.8 Ga and 56 times at 4.5 Ga, where it lit a 30-bar sky that, like its day sky, was a featureless peach glow.

5.4 Lunar eclipses

In a lunar eclipse the Moon passes through the Earth's shadow, which is lit only by sunlight bent into it through the Earth's limb: every sunrise and sunset on Earth at once. Its color and brightness are a measurement of the whole atmosphere at the terminator, which is why eclipses darkened after Tambora, Krakatoa, El Chichón and Pinatubo (Keen 1983; Stothers 2004) and dimmed measurably after the small Kasatochi eruption of 2008 (García Muñoz et al. 2011), and why the eclipsed Moon's spectrum is Earth's transmission spectrum as an exoplanet would show it (Pallé et al. 2009). The same physics, run on each epoch's air, gives the eclipse of every era.

The model (lunar_eclipse.py) traces rays from the Sun through the epoch's atmosphere at tangent heights from the ground to 120 km, bending with the refractivity of its gas mix and accumulating the optical depth of every component (gas, ozone, aerosol, sulfate, haze, soot) along the whole path, with today's cloud tops cutting the lowest rays. Seen from a point on the Moon, the Earth's limb at each position angle and height shows the Sun's limb-darkened disk wherever the ray's bending puts it; summing that over the ring of the limb (Link's method; Link 1969; García Muñoz et al. 2012 for a modern treatment) gives the spectrum of the light at each distance from the shadow's axis, and the direct sunlight past the top of the air gives the penumbra.

Today's umbra comes out a dull copper. A central eclipse puts the Moon 12.3 magnitudes below the full Moon, about V = −0.4, in the range observed for clear-air eclipses, with the center darkest and a paler, slightly bluish edge where ozone's Chappuis band removes the orange from the highest rays (the turquoise fringe of eclipse photographs). Before the Great Oxidation there is no ozone and that edge is orange too. A Tambora-sized sulfate veil puts the Moon near V = +11, a surface brightness of 27 mag/arcsec², far below the night sky: it vanishes, as it did to observers in June 1816 (Stothers 2004). The K–Pg soot and the thick Neoarchean haze remove it entirely; the thin haze leaves a dim brown-red Moon near V = +5.

Two effects are new to the deep past. The closer Moon sat nearer the Earth than the refracted light comes to a focus (about 300,000 km today, past the Moon's 384,000), so the middle of the shadow is reached only by rays skimming the ground and goes dark: at 3.8 Ga the center of the shadow is a hundred million times fainter than its edge, a dark core in a glowing ring. And the 30-bar Hadean air is so refractive that below about 19 km its rays are trapped and run round the planet, while the upper air bends light strongly enough to fill the whole umbra of a Moon some 39 Earth radii out, an even, deep red at V = −1.7; but the Moon of 4.5 Ga, only 8 Earth radii out, sits well inside the focus, and at mid-eclipse it is gone, V = +12.

The shadow's geometry follows the distances and the young Sun's size. The umbra was 3.1 Moon widths across at 4.0 Ga against 2.7 today, and with twice as many full Moons a year, total lunar eclipses came nearly three times as often, while totality itself lasted at most 104 to 109 minutes in every epoch from 4.0 Ga on (Table 6). At 4.5 Ga the Moon, inside about 17 Earth radii, orbits in the plane of the Earth's equator, its shadow is 3.6 Moon widths across and it races through it: around each equinox every full Moon is eclipsed, some 3,900 total eclipses a century, none longer than an hour. The rate also depends on the tilt of the Moon's orbit. It was a little steeper then: integrating today's 5.145° back along the distance history with the tidal model of Ćuk et al. (2016), in which Earth's tides flatten the orbit as the Moon recedes and tides raised in the Moon damp it, gives 5.46° at 2.7 Ga and 5.80° at 4.0 Ga (a little more for a Moon stiffer or more dissipative). The much larger tilts that model and Downey, Nimmo & Matsuyama (2023) need for the young Moon belong to before the Cassini-state transition near 33 Earth radii, older than any epoch here but 4.5 Ga, whose Moon is in the equator's plane (lunar_inclination.py).

The ephemeris is checked against the almanac. For the total eclipses of 2022, 2025, 2026 and 2029, contact times fall within 2 to 7 minutes of the NASA catalog (Espenak & Meeus 2009) and umbral magnitudes within 0.04 (for 2029 June 26, 1.831 against 1.844); over 2000–2100 the page finds 144 umbral and 84 total eclipses, against the catalog's 142 and 85. On the page the Moon is drawn for an eye adapted to its brightest part, so the umbra looks black beside the penumbra in a partial phase and glows in totality, as it does to an observer.

6. The planets and their moons

6.1 Where the planets were

The five naked-eye planets, Uranus and Neptune are placed from JPL's approximate Keplerian elements (Standish's table, valid 1800–2050) for the date and time, light-time corrected, on the same magnitude scale as the stars (Meeus's formulae with the phase angle, Saturn's rings included when there are rings, and Mallama & Hilton 2018 for Uranus and Neptune), and dimmed by the young Sun's fainter light: 0.42 magnitudes at 4.5 Ga, 0.24 at 2.7 Ga. Any planet brighter than magnitude −6 lights the sky as the Moon does. In the historical and modern skies the positions are the real ones. Before history they cannot be known: the Solar System is chaotic, its uncertainties growing tenfold every ten million years or so (Laskar 1989), and every epoch's age is uncertain by far more than any planet's period. So each planet is put at a random place on its orbit, the same for every visit to an epoch, and moves on with the date. The orbits' shapes are today's, known to some 50 million years and statistically before.

The two oldest skies have a different Solar System. In the reading of the meteorites' bombardment ages (Edwards et al. 2024; Liu, Raymond & Jacobson 2022), the giant planets went unstable early, within the first 100 million years; the 4.55 Ga sky shows them before it, in the best starting configuration of Nesvorný & Morbidelli (2012): Jupiter at 5.6 AU and Saturn at 7.34 AU in a 3:2 resonance, a fifth giant at 9.62 AU, Uranus at 15.3 and Neptune at 20 AU, each in resonance with the next. The fifth giant, an ice giant like Neptune that Jupiter threw out of the Solar System in the instability (Nesvorný 2011), is named here Oceanus. For the 4.5 Ga sky we take the instability to have come late enough, near 4.5 Ga, to keep it; the bombardment ages argue against that, as the 4.55 Ga sky's account says.

Theia, the Mars-sized body whose collision with the proto-Earth made the Moon, is a wandering planet in the 4.55 Ga sky. Its orbit is made up, as any that would meet the Earth's will do, since where it lay is not known (Branco, Raymond & Machado 2025). Every 25 years or so it passes within a few hundredths of an AU, and at its closest it reaches magnitude −8.5, half lit, brighter than any planet has been since, lighting the night. Its face is invented too: an airless, cratered, iron-rich basaltic crust (Meier, Reufer & Wieler 2014), its steam atmosphere lost to the young Sun within a few tens of millions of years (Odert et al. 2018), with eight great basins and a few young rayed craters.

6.2 The planets close up

Zooming in acts as a telescope, gaining 5 magnitudes against the sky for each tenfold zoom (magnification spreads the sky's light and leaves a point a point), so faint moons and Uranus and Neptune come out, and Mercury and Venus show by day. Each planet is a disk of its true angular size and flattening, on its IAU pole and prime meridian, lit from the Sun's side, so the phases of Mercury and Venus show; its limb darkens by a Minnaert law. Mercury and Mars wear spacecraft maps, MESSENGER's color mosaic and Viking's, toned toward true color, with their relief from MESSENGER (Becker et al. 2016) and the Mars Orbiter Laser Altimeter: slopes lit by the planet's own law, and rims and peaks hiding the Sun, so a gibbous Mars shows the shadows of Tharsis and Olympus Mons near its terminator and a half-lit Mercury a ragged, cratered one. Venus is cloud, cream and featureless, bright in the crescent. The moons of Jupiter and Saturn, and Triton, have their own maps (Galileo, Voyager and Cassini mosaics), and cast their shadows on their planets, go dark in the planets' shadows, and pass behind and in front of them. Figure 8 shows every rocky surface the site draws.

6.3 Jupiter

Jupiter close up is drawn, not mapped: its clouds change too fast for any one map to stand for an epoch. The bands lie where the Cassini wind profile (Porco et al. 2003) puts its jets, and the clouds are a tracer stirred by eddies: each point is followed back along the streamlines of a stream function of noise, three octaves of cells three times longer along the winds than across, renewing at different times, its strength greatest in the belts and toward the poles and coming and going in storm patches some 45° long. The flow keeps area, so the belts and zones and the finer banding within them marble into curls and filaments rather than creases, and the jets' own shear draws them out along the bands. Along each boundary between a belt and a zone, Kelvin–Helmholtz billows roll up, turning the way of the shear there. Dark festoons trail from the North Equatorial Belt into the Equatorial Zone with blue-gray hot spots at their heads; dark barges sit on the belt's northern edge, and white ovals in the South South Temperate Belt. The tracer approach follows the flow-field techniques of Dziewanowski (2024).

The Great Red Spot is a vortex in the same flow: an anticyclone turning the clouds along its ellipses, faster toward its edge, with a slight inflow that draws belt and zone onto its rim as spiral arms, and its turbulent wake to the west. Its history is the observed one. It was first seen for sure in 1831 (Cassini's “permanent spot” of 1665–1713 may have been another storm), so the 1815 sky has none. Its longitude follows the measured record (Peek's for 1831–1952, JUPOS since), and its size the fits of Simon et al. (2018) from 1979, 405.0 − 0.1939 Y degrees long and 107.2 − 0.0483 Y wide, and before 1979 a steady shrinking from about 35° long in the 1880s. The fits meet in a round spot 8.4° across in 2045, and it is held there for 2100: whether it shrinks on, steadies or fades is not known. It was reddest in 1879–1882 and has deepened again since 2014. In the deep past there is no Red Spot: storms like it come and go over centuries.

6.4 Saturn and its rings

Saturn close up is drawn as Jupiter is, a tracer stirred by the same flow, with its own winds, bands and colors. The winds are Cassini's at the cloud tops in 2004–2009 (García-Melendo et al. 2011), fit by twenty Gaussian jets to 6 m/s rms in System III, which also turns the planet: the broad equatorial jet near 400 m/s, and narrower jets alternating with latitude toward the poles. The belts lie where the wind falls off poleward, as Jupiter's do, the broad pair at 18–32° and fainter, narrower ones beyond. Saturn's haze mutes all of it, so the eddies stir about half as hard as Jupiter's, the billows turn less, and the hues vary a half to a third as much. Around the north pole the jet at 78°N meanders in a standing wave of six, the hexagon (Godfrey 1988), golden inside in the northern summer and bluish gray in the winter; both poles have a vortex with a dark eye and a bright wall, a thin ribbon wave runs along the jet at 47°N, and small bright storms rise in Storm Alley near 40°S. The winter hemisphere, out of the Sun, shows bluish at any size, as Cassini saw the north before 2009. That change lags the season by several years, and the lag is not drawn.

Saturn's rings are drawn from the Cassini radio occultation of 3 May 2005 (Marouf et al.), its optical depth at 10 km resolution from the C ring to the outer A ring, corrected to visible light in the C ring, the Cassini division and the outer A ring by the Ka-band occultation (whose sub-centimetre particles Jerousek et al. 2016 find), with the F ring added. Each ring is a single-scattering layer (as Cuzzi et al. 1984): lit from the Sun's side it shines by its depth and particle brightness, the A ring 0.7 of the B ring's and the C ring and Cassini division half of it and grayer; seen from the unlit side only light passing through it shows, so the B ring is black and the C ring and Cassini division glow. The rings shadow the globe, and the globe shadows the rings with its oblate outline and a penumbra the Sun's width. Near the equinoxes, when the Sun is low over the rings, they shadow the moons too: a moon passing behind them is banded by their shadow and dimmed by what they let through, Mimas by up to 4 magnitudes deep in the B ring's. Edge-on, the rings thin below a pixel.

The rings are young. How young is still argued, 100 to 400 million years (Iess et al. 2019; Kempf et al. 2023), and we adopt the account of Wisdom et al. (2022): an icy moon the size of Iapetus, named Chrysalis, orbiting between Titan and Iapetus in a 3:1 resonance with Titan, was torn apart about 160 million years ago, freeing Saturn's tilt from Neptune's pull and making the rings of its debris. So the rings appear in the 66 Ma sky and after, and before them Chrysalis is a moon of magnitude 13 to 14 beside a ringless Saturn. Younger rings are drawn more massive and cleaner: their depth grows with youth as age⁻⁰·⁷⁵, between ring-rain losses (O'Donoghue et al. 2019; Waite et al. 2018) and viscous spreading (Salmon et al. 2010), half again today's at 66 Ma, and the meteoroid darkening of the C ring and Cassini division (Cuzzi & Estrada 1998) is two fifths of today's. Both are guesses. Saturn's pole precesses once in about 1.87 million years (Ward & Hamilton 2004), so the rings open from a different direction at each epoch: by a known angle at the Pleistocene supernovae, at random beyond ten million years.

6.5 The planets' moons

The moons with fitted orbits, fitted here to JPL Horizons over 1980–2060, are Io, Europa, Ganymede and Callisto; Mimas, Enceladus, Tethys, Dione, Rhea, Titan and Iapetus; Miranda, Ariel, Umbriel, Titania and Oberon; and Triton. Most hold to a tenth of a degree. Iapetus's two faces show: its trailing side is ten times brighter than its leading side, so it is magnitude 10.2 at western elongation and 11.9 at eastern. The planets' moons also change with the epoch. Triton, retrograde, was captured in the giant-planet instability, so the two oldest skies lack it, and Neptune has instead a family of regular moons, here named Kymo, Galene, Thetis and Amphitrite, drawn like Uranus's four largest at the same distances: Rufu & Canup (2017) find that a system no heavier than Uranus's fits best, and that capturing Triton scattered and destroyed it. Mars, at 4.0 and 3.8 Ga, has Harmonia (named here), the moon of some twenty times Phobos's mass at 3.3 Mars radii that Ćuk et al. (2020) find tilted Deimos's orbit, one generation of Mars's cycle of rings and moons (Hesselbrock & Minton 2017). Phobos and Deimos themselves, too faint to matter, are not drawn.

7. The stars and the Galaxy

7.1 The stars moved back

Today's sky has the thousand brightest stars of the Yale Bright Star Catalogue (Hoffleit & Warren 1991), down to about magnitude 4.6, carried to the year shown by proper motion and precession, each tinted by its color temperature and shown only when it is brighter than the naked-eye limit for the sky around it, so stars come out one by one in twilight and cities keep only the brightest. Earth's axis keeps today's tilt and direction in every epoch, since its precession in the deep past cannot be pinned down. Going back, the stars move, and how far the page can follow them sets three kinds of sky.

For the Pleistocene supernovae, 1.78 Ma and 342 ka, every catalogue star is moved in a straight line from its Hipparcos parallax, proper motion and radial velocity (the XHIP compilation of Anderson & Francis 2012), and the thousand brightest at that time are kept. Over two million years the Galaxy's pull bends their paths by only a few parsecs. The sky is recognizable but rearranged. At 1.78 Ma Canopus is the brightest star, −1.6, and Sirius, far away then, is fourth magnitude; at 342 ka Aldebaran, near its closest pass, outshines everything at −1.5, and Sirius is +0.8. Constellation figures move with their stars, and a line is dropped once its stars have drifted three times today's distance apart.

At 66 Ma the Sun and the catalogue stars are traced back along orbits in a model Galaxy: a flat rotation curve of 233 km/s, a vertical oscillation of 84 million years, and the Sun's motion from Schönrich, Binney & Dehnen (2010), keeping only stars old enough to have been shining. Six of them were brighter than magnitude 4.6. Further back none of today's neighbors was near the Sun, and every star is a stand-in: a copy of a star of today's sky, keeping its brightness, color, spectral type and galactic latitude, at a random galactic longitude, a different random sky for each age. The stand-ins' labels give the type they copy, not a name. The sky's statistics are right; its patterns are invented, as they would be for any reconstruction that far back.

7.2 Stars brighter than Sirius

Sirius, at magnitude −1.46, is the brightest star in today's night sky, but it has not always been. The Sun's neighbours drift past it at tens of kilometres a second, so a star a hundred parsecs away now may have passed within a few parsecs of it a few million years ago. Tracing every Hipparcos star that has a radial velocity back 10 Myr through the Galaxy, with 2,000 draws over each star's measurement errors, finds eleven that outshone today's Sirius (Table 7). The brightest is θ Columbae, a fifth-magnitude star today, which passed about 2 pc from the Sun 4.7 million years ago and peaked near magnitude −5, as bright as Venus at its best; Gaia DR3 astrometry gives the same (−5.2 at 2.1 pc, 5.1 million years ago). ε Canis Majoris reached −4.35 4.4 million years ago, a result known since Tomkin (1998), and β Canis Majoris −3.6 at the same time. From about 3.5 to 5 million years ago the night sky held at least two stars brighter than any star today, and at times three.

These stars now lie in Columba, Canis Major and Puppis because that is the solar antapex: the Sun moves toward Hercules at about 20 km/s relative to its neighbours, so the stars it has passed end up behind it. The closest pass, ζ Leporis at 1.3 pc 850,000 years ago, came as close as α Centauri is now, far too distant to disturb the planets. Only distance changes the brightness here. ε and β Canis Majoris are giants 12 to 22 million years old and were probably a few tenths of a magnitude fainter then. Algol's radial velocity (3.7 ± 3.9 km/s, hard to measure in an eclipsing binary) is too uncertain to say whether it passed within 1.3 or 28 pc of the Sun. Rigel, Saiph, Mintaka, Alnitak and ξ Persei also come out bright, but 6 to 10 million years ago, about their own ages, so they are left out. The site's skies do not show these peaks: the supernova epochs (1.78 Ma and 342 ka) fall between them, though at 342 ka Aldebaran is close to its peak of −1.5.

7.3 The Milky Way, nebulae and galaxies

The Milky Way is a model in galactic coordinates rather than a photograph: a disk and bulge, the Sagittarius and Scutum star clouds, the Great Rift from Cygnus to Sagittarius, the Coalsack and the Ophiuchus and Taurus dust, peaking at 20.2 mag/arcsec² in the Sagittarius star cloud (Leinert et al. 1998), and shown only in a dark sky. In the older skies its brightest part lies where the Galactic center then lay as seen from the Sun, from the Sun's orbit traced back through the same model Galaxy, and the band shifts by a few degrees with the Sun's height above the plane: at 66 Ma the Sun was 100 pc north of it. Beyond about a billion years the Sun's place on its orbit is only nominal. The Galaxy's own structure is today's in every epoch.

The 34 nebulae and galaxies that binoculars show under a dark sky are drawn from survey photographs, their stars taken out, each scaled to its catalogue magnitude and surface brightness, and turning into its photograph when zoomed. They change with the epoch. The Andromeda and Triangulum galaxies fall toward the Milky Way on a timing-argument orbit (van der Marel et al. 2012; Kahn & Woltjer 1959), so at 4.5 Ga Andromeda is three quarters of today's size. The Large Magellanic Cloud is on its first infall (Kallivayalil et al. 2013), traced back through the Galaxy's halo with dynamical friction: a small patch in another part of the sky in the Hadean, larger than today's at 66 Ma. Galaxies beyond the Local Group were nearer by the cosmic scale factor. The nebulae are young: each is drawn only within its age, so the Orion Nebula is absent at 1.78 Ma, and none of today's shine at 66 Ma or before, when others, unknowable, did.

7.4 Supernovae

Two skies are lit by a supernova. Geminga's, about 342,000 years ago by its pulsar's spin-down age (Salvati & Sacco 2008), exploded 90 to 240 pc away toward Orion (Pellizza et al. 2005); a typical Type II-P peaks near absolute magnitude −16.75 (Richardson et al. 2014), so from 147 pc it reached about −11, a fifth of the full Moon's light from a single point, bright enough to show by day and cast shadows at night for the three months of its plateau. The ζ Ophiuchi supernova, 1.78 million years ago at 107 pc in the Scorpius–Centaurus association (Neuhäuser et al. 2020), unbound its companion, now the runaway star ζ Oph, and peaked near −11.6, twice as bright. Its spectrum readout is a Type II-P near peak, with P Cygni profiles from fast ejecta (Filippenko 1997). At these distances neither touches the sky's colors (Thomas et al. 2016).

8. The night and what crosses it

8.1 Twilight and the night sky

Because the photometric scale of Section 2 is absolute, the night is drawn on the same scale as the day. The sky is computed for Sun heights down to 20° below the horizon; past 9° below, where the model's twilight fades too slowly, we make it dim by about a magnitude per degree, as measured. Without the Sun or Moon the sky has its own light: today 22.0 mag/arcsec² at a dark zenith (Leinert et al. 1998), half of it starlight and zodiacal light and half airglow, brighter toward the horizon.

Nearly all of today's airglow needs free oxygen: the 557.7 nm green and 630 nm red lines of oxygen atoms, the hydroxyl bands (H + O₃), the sodium D lines cycled through ozone, and the NO₂ continuum. We take it as 90% of today's at 466 Ma, 80% in the Snowball epoch (169 DU of ozone and less O₂), and 30% at 2.2 Ga, where 1% of today's oxygen leaves few atoms near 95 km. Before the Great Oxidation it is gone, replaced by a faint violet glow of the O₂ Herzberg II bands from oxygen split off CO₂, as on Venus (Krasnopolsky 1983): about as many photons as today's airglow but only 15% of its luminance, so Archean and Hadean nights were darker and bluer. These strengths are estimates; no model of an anoxic nightglow exists.

Starlight, the Milky Way and the airglow all come from above the air and are dimmed by it, at the rate given in Section 2: 0.25 magnitude per airmass in clean air, 0.8 under the thick haze or a polluted city, 0.85 under the proto-Earth's guessed air and dust, 2.3 through the impact-winter soot, and 7.6 under 30 bar of CO₂, which hides every star.

8.2 Aurorae

The aurora is an oval round the magnetic pole, fixed relative to the Sun: on a moderately active night today (Kp 3) it spans about 63–72° latitude on the night side (Feldstein's ovals). Its field lines reach out to the magnetopause, whose distance goes as the sixth root of the field's pressure over the solar wind's. At 3.45 Ga a field half to 70% of today's and the young Sun's dense wind held the magnetopause at about half today's distance (Tarduno et al. 2010), which brings the oval's edge down to about 50° even in quiet times, and the young Sun's frequent flares and mass ejections (Airapetian et al. 2016) make storms the usual state. Through the Proterozoic the wind weakens (Wood et al. 2005) and the oval retreats toward the pole.

The colors follow the air. Today's green and red lines are oxygen atoms. At 2.2 Ga they are about a third of today's. With no free oxygen the aurora is nitrogen's: violet N₂⁺ bands and a pink border of N₂ first positive bands where faster electrons reach lowest, brighter without oxygen to quench them, with a weak green line from CO₂ split by the electrons, as Perseverance saw on Mars (Knutsen et al. 2025). The 30-bar Hadean air is mostly CO₂, so there the green line would be stronger and the nitrogen faint, but the air, at 7.6 magnitudes of extinction per airmass, hides the aurora altogether. Brightness is for a dark-adapted eye, which sees violet far better than the deep red. The ancient line strengths are estimates.

Each night has its own activity about the epoch's typical level, and the oval is drawn at it. Today that is Kp 3; the young Sun's typical night is far stormier, Kp 6 at 4.0 Ga, and its oval reaches correspondingly lower, to about 37° on the night side at 4.0 Ga and 43° at 3.8 Ga (Table 8 gives both). The arcs are thin sheets along the field lines, green below and red above, with field-aligned rays converging overhead on the magnetic zenith; they fold, drift and break up in two substorms a night near midnight. A storm of the class of September 1859, when aurora stood overhead near 40° magnetic latitude, brings today's oval down to about 45° and the young Earth's to the equator.

8.3 Meteors and meteor showers

Each meteor is a meteoroid entering the air along a straight path 80 to 125 km up, with its brightness, size and speed tied by the photographic relation of Jacchia, Verniani & Briggs (1967) and its count set by the measured fireball rate. Today a dark site sees about 8 an hour, more before dawn. A meteor shows only when brighter than the sky around it, so twilight, moonlight and city light thin them out. The air enters three ways. Bright, fast meteors leave persistent trains that glow green and then orange; that chemistry needs oxygen and ozone, so there are no trains before the Great Oxidation. Each meteor's color comes from a spectrum built for its speed and the epoch's air: the metals of the meteoroid, a hotter component that grows with speed, and the air's own emission, oxygen and nitrogen today or carbon monoxide bands in a CO₂-rich air, which no one has measured. And in the Early Hadean's 30 bar every density level sits higher, so meteors burn about 22 km higher up.

The rate follows the lunar cratering record (Neukum et al. 2001): about 10,000 times today's at 4.5 Ga, in the giant impact's debris, 500 at 4.0 Ga and 120 at 3.8 Ga, of slow, yellow-orange fireballs from a main-belt-like population (Strom et al. 2015; Marchi et al. 2014), with impact flashes on the closer Moon's dark side; twice today's at 2.7 Ga; and a hundred times today's fireballs at 466 Ma, after the L-chondrite parent body broke up (Schmitz et al. 2019).

Meteor showers come on their own dates. The modern-era skies have the 38 showers of the IMO's working list (Rendtel 2027), with their radiants and drift, speeds, population indices and peak rates, rising and falling about the maximum as Jenniskens (1994) measured them, and their outbursts and storms at the hour they were seen: the Leonids of 1799 to 2002, the Andromedids of 1872 and 1885, the Draconids of 1933 and 1946 and others (Jenniskens 1995 and the IMO's analyses), with the Leonid peaks predicted for 2034. Showers last thousands of years, so the older epochs have their own, drawn at random with the geometry, speeds and profiles of today's and outbursts at today's rate, about 0.5 a year above ZHR 100 and one in 45 years above 10,000. We take their number to follow the comets that feed them: three quarters from short-period comets, a quarter from long-period ones (only about a fifth of known streams have an identified parent; Ye & Jenniskens 2024), giving about 30 times today's at 4.5 Ga, 5 at 4.0 Ga, today's by 2 Ga and 1.75 at 1.78 Ma, in the comet shower after a star's passage. No published work estimates showers in the early Solar System, so these are estimates, and in the bombardment they hardly show against the sporadic rate.

8.4 Fireballs and impacts

The largest meteoroids do not burn up. Bodies a meter across and more come in as superbolides, brighter than magnitude −15, and leave dust trails from about 80 km down to where they break up at 25 to 40 km, which drift and shear in the high winds, as Chelyabinsk's did for over an hour (Borovička et al. 2013); today about one comes within 1,100 km of a given place every three years, and in the bombardment several an hour. Bodies brighter than about −24 reach the ground. When one strikes within 200 km it is drawn with its fireball, a thermal pulse cooling from 6,500 to 2,000 K, the blast wave, a condensation ring and the rising cloud, scaled from nuclear-test and impact-effect relations (Glasstone & Dolan 1977; Collins, Melosh & Marcus 2005). Today that happens to a given place about once in 50,000 years; in the bombardment, constantly. In the bombardment epochs, impact flashes also show on the closer Moon's night side, at today's measured rate scaled up (Suggs et al. 2014).

8.5 Dust, comets and the Ordovician ring

The zodiacal light, sunlight off interplanetary dust, is part of today's natural night sky. Where the inner Solar System held more dust the excess is drawn along the ecliptic, with the gegenschein opposite the Sun: 30 times today's after the L-chondrite break-up and 50 to 1,000 times during the bombardment (estimates after Nesvorný et al. 2010), as bright as a moonlit sky, hiding the fainter stars and meteors. At 466 Ma the speculative debris ring of Tomkins, Martin & Cawood (2024) is drawn between 1.55 and 2.75 Earth radii with a normal optical depth of at most 0.00015: lost in the blue by day, a low arch at night cut by the Earth's shadow, and at the equator a source of slow, grazing fireballs from the west.

Comets in the modern-era skies are the real ones on their real dates, from JPL's orbits; elsewhere they are drawn at the rate of their time, about one naked-eye comet a year today, 30 times that at 4.5 Ga while the giant planets eroded and then scattered the comet disk, falling to today's level by about 2 Ga, and 0.6 of today's in the quiet Phanerozoic epochs, since today's sky may still hold the comet shower from the star HD 7977 (Kaib & Raymond 2026). Their heads and tails are dimmed by each epoch's air like the stars.

9. The sky people made

9.1 City light

In the modern epochs the observer stands in a mid-sized city: a zenith glow of 18.8 mag/arcsec² today (Falchi et al. 2016), with orange sodium light in 1980–2000 (Cinzano, Falchi & Elvidge 2001), 1.6 times today's in polluted air, held at today's level in 2100 (the recent 9.6% a year, Kyba et al. 2023, cannot be projected that far), and almost nothing from the oil lamps of 1815 (Fouquet & Pearson 2006). The glow rises about threefold toward the horizon, and cloud bases over the city glow orange several times brighter than the clear sky (Kyba et al. 2011). Against that glow the city keeps only the brightest stars, and none of the Milky Way.

9.2 The sky before electric light

The 1815 sky is the last before gas and electric street lighting. Its towns burn oil lamps and candles: Britain then used about one six-thousand-five-hundredth of the artificial light per head that it used in 2000 (Fouquet & Pearson 2006), so the town's glow on the sky is some ten thousand times fainter than a modern city's, and the Milky Way stands over the rooftops.

9.3 Aircraft

The modern-era skies have airliners and their contrails: about 1.1 aircraft over each 10,000 km² of busy mid-latitude sky by day, from European traffic statistics, at 9 to 12 km along a few airways, quieter after midnight; under half of today's traffic in 1990, twice today's in 2100, none in 1815. A contrail forms where the exhaust's mixing line crosses saturation (Schmidt 1941; Appleman 1953), most often at mid and high latitudes, and lives seconds in dry air but spreads into contrail cirrus lasting hours in the 10 to 20% of cruise levels that are supersaturated with respect to ice (Gierens et al. 1999; Schumann 2005; Minnis et al. 1998). At night the aircraft show as their navigation lights, beacon and strobes.

9.4 Satellites

The 2100 sky has today's air and the satellites that may fill it. Lawler, Boley & Rein (2022) put every filed megaconstellation on orbit, 65,262 satellites in 30 shells from 328 to 1,200 km, and found the worst naked-eye light pollution near 50° latitude; each is drawn as their diffuse sphere of 0.8 m² effective area, so its magnitude is on the stars' scale. At the equinox a mid-latitude sky has a few hundred of them above naked-eye brightness in the hour after sunset, and the Earth's shadow takes them by midnight. On top of that fleet are the orbital datacenters modeled by Boley, Lawler & Rein (2026). Of their three filed designs we take the middle one and the more optimistic of their two node spreads: Blue Origin's Sunrise, 51,600 Sun-synchronous satellites from 500 to 1,800 km in a dawn–dusk cross of rings whose nodes wander 10° to either side of the terminator. Each is a diffuse sphere of 800 m² at albedo 0.2, the size they call conservative next to panels several times larger, and two hundred times a communications satellite's reflecting area. An hour after sunset, thousands of them are above naked-eye brightness, a bright band along the terminator, each crossing the dome in minutes. The paper's all-night winter rings belong to the December solstice, which the page's equinox geometry does not show.

10. Epoch by epoch

The panels that follow are laid out identically so they can be compared at a glance. Each begins with the epoch's name and a one-line summary of the atmosphere assumed (Table 2 gives the full parameters). The upper row shows the noon sky dome at three latitudes, the equator, a mid-latitude site and the summer pole, with the zenith at the top of each swatch and the horizon at the bottom, the correlated color temperatures of both, and the Sun's disk drawn in its own color at its noon elevation, with a brightness that reflects how much of it survives the atmosphere. The two strips beneath trace the sky from the solar horizon across the zenith to the antisolar horizon with the Sun on the horizon and 4° below it. All swatches are shown at a brightness relative to today's clean sky, so a dim epoch reads as dim. The paragraph after each panel describes that epoch's sky and what else was in it.

Some 17 million years after the first solids, the gas of the Sun's disk has just cleared, and with it, in the reading of the meteorites' bombardment ages (Edwards et al. 2024; Liu, Raymond & Jacobson 2022), the giant planets have yet to go unstable, or are about to. Jupiter and Saturn sit in 3:2 resonance near 5.6 and 7.3 AU, and beyond them three ice giants: Uranus and Neptune, nearer than now, and between them and Saturn a fifth giant like Neptune, named here Oceanus, which Jupiter will throw out of the Solar System (Nesvorný 2011; Nesvorný & Morbidelli 2012). Neptune still has its own family of regular moons, named here Kymo, Galene, Thetis and Amphitrite; capturing Triton will scatter and destroy them (Rufu & Canup 2017). There is no Moon: the Earth is still growing, and Theia, the Mars-sized body that will strike it and make the Moon, is a wandering planet near the Earth's orbit, brighter than Venus when it passes close. The Sun is a pre-main-sequence star 17 million years old (Baraffe et al. 2015): 4,600 K, half today's light, a cooler, oranger disk 7% larger. Nothing constrains the proto-Earth's air; we take it as 3 bar of CO₂ over a bar of nitrogen, with dust from the impacts, so the sky can be seen through it. Where each planet was on any day cannot be known.

About ten million years after the Moon-forming impact. The magma ocean has frozen, the steam of the impact has rained out into the first ocean, and tens of bars of CO₂ are left in the air, which we take as 30 bar. A ~30-bar CO₂ atmosphere has a Rayleigh optical depth near 5 at 550 nm and about 18 in the violet, so blue light is scattered back to space many times before it reaches the ground. What arrives is a diffuse, shadowless, peach-white glow of ~3,300 K, nearly identical from zenith to horizon, under a young Sun that is only 68% as bright. The Sun itself is a dim ember at the equator and vanishes entirely at mid and high latitudes: this is a Venus-like sky. Sunset is a brief, deep-orange dimming of the whole dome rather than an event at the horizon. Above it, the Moon is still only about 8 Earth radii away (Korenaga 2023): 4° across, seven and a half times its width today and 56 times its area, its own magma ocean still open, glowing orange through cracks in its crust, and going round the Earth in 32 hours in the plane of the equator, while the Earth turns in under 6. It crosses the sky in hours, and for weeks around each equinox it eclipses the Sun at every new Moon, somewhere on the Earth, and passes through the Earth's shadow, 14° across at its distance, at every full Moon. Tidal recession will carry it out to about 39 Earth radii by 4.4 Ga. For this epoch we assume the giant planets' instability came late enough, near 4.5 Ga, that the fifth giant, Oceanus, and Neptune's first moons are still here; the bombardment ages favour an earlier one (Edwards et al. 2024), as in the 4.55 Ga sky. Through 30 bar of CO₂ no star shows; the planets and their moons are there to be found by zooming in. The Sun is 67 million years old, near the main sequence: 5,500 K and 68% of today's light.

Once most of the CO₂ has gone into carbonate, Rayleigh scattering falls to roughly twice the modern value. The sky turns pale blue at the zenith but clearly whiter than today (7,000–10,500 K versus 9,000–15,000 K), because the extra scattering fills the dome with multiply-scattered white light. Horizons are milky. The setting Sun is deep red and the twilight zenith, with no ozone yet, is cream rather than blue.

With CO₂ down to ~0.1 bar, noon skies are close to modern blue, only slightly whiter. The difference is at dusk. The blue of the modern twilight zenith is produced by ozone absorbing yellow-orange light (the Chappuis band) along the long grazing path; with no free O₂ there is no ozone, so the Archean twilight zenith is a pale yellow-cream, and the whole sky fades from blue to beige to orange as the Sun sets. Sunsets themselves are much like today's, slightly redder from the extra CO₂ and dimmer Sun.

An intermittent organic haze at optical depth ~0.15 pushes the zenith toward a pastel, milk-blue (7,000–8,500 K) and lays a warm cast on the horizon; at the poles, where sunlight crosses the haze obliquely, the horizon turns visibly cream. Twilight is orange all the way to the zenith.

This is the “Pale Orange Dot” seen from below. At optical depth ~0.6 the haze absorbs blue and scatters forward, so the entire dome is a warm cream to pale tan (~5,300 K at the equator, ~4,700 K at the poles) with almost no zenith-to-horizon gradient: the sky looks like a bright overcast made of orange-tinted glass. The Sun is a soft, defined disk (haze scatters strongly forward) at 4,100 K. Sunsets are deep and long: the solar horizon reaches vermilion, the sky 15° above the Sun is amber, and the antisolar sky is peach rather than pink.

At the upper end of plausible haze (τ≈1.5) the sky is a uniform saturated apricot (3,300–4,200 K), as on Titan, and the polar Sun is reduced to an orange smear. The ground under it gets roughly 20–30% of a clear sky's sunlight.

After the Great Oxidation Event, about 1% of today's O₂ builds an ozone column of 66 DU, the Cooke et al. (2022) global mean for that oxygen level: about a fifth of a modern mid-latitude column, not the half that older estimates gave. Noon skies are already modern blue. Twilight is where the thin column shows. With the Sun 4° below the horizon the zenith leaves the cream of an ozone-free dusk (~6,000 K) and becomes a pale blue-gray (~7,100 K). It is not yet the deep blue of a 300 DU twilight (~12,500 K). That saturated blue dusk is in place once the column is near modern, as in the snowball sky at 169 DU. (The pink antisolar arch needs no ozone: it is a Rayleigh effect and shows up faintly even in the Hadean model.)

A frozen planet has dry, clean air and a surface albedo near 0.75, and together they give the bluest sky in Earth's history: 9,000 K at the equatorial zenith and over 20,000 K over polar ice, with horizons that stay distinctly blue instead of whitening, because the sunlit ice floods the sky from below with blue-white light. Sunsets are golden and comparatively pale; there is little aerosol to redden them.
